s4.daily.childhood.1: Rain taps the window. You move a finger beside one drop and follow it to the sill.
s4.daily.childhood.2: You build a room from cushions. The doorway is just wide enough for your favorite toy.
s4.daily.childhood.3: Your shadow stretches across the ground. You change your steps to see it move.
s4.daily.childhood.4: You fill a page with color. One mark goes beyond the edge, and you make it part of the picture.
s4.daily.childhood.5: A familiar tune begins nearby. You join in with the part you recognize.
s4.daily.childhood.6: You give a toy a name. When you put it away, you say the name once more.
s4.daily.childhood.7: A seed has opened in a small pot. You bring it closer to the light.
s4.daily.childhood.8: An empty box becomes a vehicle in your game. Its first journey stays inside the room.
s4.daily.childhood.9: You sort a few belongings into places of your own. Finding them later feels a little easier.
s4.daily.childhood.10: You compare a leaf with a smooth stone. You keep noticing how different they feel.
s4.daily.childhood.11: You pause by an open doorway. A sound outside becomes something you want to ask about.
s4.daily.childhood.12: At a meal you try an unfamiliar flavor. You take time to decide whether you like it.
s4.daily.childhood.13: A small fastening takes several tries. This time your hands find where it belongs.
s4.daily.childhood.14: You collect a few small treasures in a box. Each has a reason that matters to you.
s4.daily.childhood.15: You invent an adventure using things within reach. You decide where this part of the story ends.
s4.daily.childhood.16: Evening changes the color of the room. You watch one bright patch become softer.
s4.daily.childhood.17: You choose a quiet corner to sit in. For a little while, watching is enough.
s4.daily.childhood.18: You arrange small objects in a pattern. One space is left for the next thing you might find.
s4.daily.childhood.19: You try a small task again after getting it wrong. This attempt works differently from the first.
s4.daily.childhood.20: You put one ordinary object somewhere safe. For today, it is the thing you want to keep.
s4.daily.study.1: A question stays with you after class. You mark the place instead of pretending you understood it.
s4.daily.study.2: You explain part of a lesson in your own words. A confusing sentence becomes a little clearer.
s4.daily.study.3: You return to a page you once skipped. You recognize one step that used to stop you.
s4.daily.study.4: You write a short study plan. There is space beside it for changing your mind after trying.
s4.daily.study.5: One topic keeps drawing you back to a book. You read a little beyond the assigned page.
s4.daily.study.6: A borrowed book shows you a useful method. You try it before deciding whether it suits you.
s4.daily.study.7: You ask about a step you did not understand. Saying it aloud takes more courage than writing a note.
s4.daily.study.8: You make a small example with your hands. The idea becomes easier to see outside the textbook.
s4.daily.study.9: You keep a little time for a difficult exercise. You finish one part and mark the rest for later.
s4.daily.study.10: You compare two explanations of the same idea. You write down where they differ.
s4.daily.study.11: You notice a mistake in an earlier answer. You correct the step without tearing up the whole page.
s4.daily.study.12: You choose one example to review before a test. Doing a small part carefully steadies the rest of the hour.
s4.daily.study.13: A lesson takes longer than you expected. You leave a note about where to begin next time.
s4.daily.study.14: You use an everyday object to understand a lesson. The object becomes a reminder of how you learned it.
s4.daily.study.15: You gather scattered notes into one place. One unfinished question gets its own heading.
s4.daily.study.16: You practice a part that once felt impossible. Today it is still slow, but no longer unfamiliar.
s4.daily.study.17: You look back at an early exercise. You can point to one thing you would now do differently.
s4.daily.study.18: You stop copying an explanation word for word. Your own rough version says more about what you understand.
s4.daily.study.19: You finish a shared classroom task. You keep a note of the part you contributed.
s4.daily.study.20: You put a completed exercise beside an unfinished one. Both belong to the same period of learning.
s4.daily.friendship.1: You and {person} talk after a shared task. A small detail becomes a joke you both recognize.
s4.daily.friendship.2: {person} asks about something you mentioned earlier. You are surprised that the detail was remembered.
s4.daily.friendship.3: You and {person} spend a quiet part of the day together. Neither has to fill every pause.
s4.daily.friendship.4: You show {person} an unfinished attempt. The conversation stays with the attempt instead of a score.
s4.daily.friendship.5: {person} tells you about a difficult small task. You listen without having a ready answer.
s4.daily.friendship.6: You and {person} remember the first task you did together. You disagree about one harmless detail.
s4.daily.friendship.7: You save a note from {person}. It is ordinary enough that someone else might have thrown it away.
s4.daily.friendship.8: You ask {person} a question you had kept to yourself. The answer opens a different part of the conversation.
s4.daily.friendship.9: You and {person} make a small shared plan. You write it down as a plan, with room for either person to change it.
s4.daily.friendship.10: You explain a boundary to {person}. A friendship can include saying what does not work for you.
s4.daily.friendship.11: {person} shares a small success. You ask how it happened instead of comparing it with your own progress.
s4.daily.friendship.12: You and {person} exchange practical help. You keep track of what happened without turning it into a debt.
s4.daily.friendship.13: You notice that your interests and {person}'s are different. You find one small thing you can still talk about.
s4.daily.friendship.14: You and {person} revisit a shared mistake. It is easier to speak about it with some time between you and that day.
s4.daily.friendship.15: You keep a brief greeting from {person}. Not every contact has to become a long conversation.
s4.daily.friendship.16: You and {person} finish a conversation without solving everything. You both know which part is still open.
s4.daily.friendship.17: {person} asks for a little space. You leave the next message unsent for now.
s4.daily.friendship.18: You return something you borrowed from {person}. A small thank-you stays attached to an ordinary errand.
s4.daily.friendship.19: You and {person} share a memory from before your lives changed. It does not require either life to return to that time.
s4.daily.friendship.20: You write down one thing you learned from knowing {person}. It is specific to this connection, not a rule about everyone.
s4.daily.family.1: You and {person} share an ordinary meal. One remark stays with you after the dishes are put away.
s4.daily.family.2: {person} shows you an old object. You ask which part of its story they want to tell.
s4.daily.family.3: You and {person} do a small household task together. Being useful is only one part of spending time nearby.
s4.daily.family.4: You listen to a familiar story from {person}. This time you notice a detail you had missed.
s4.daily.family.5: You tell {person} about an ordinary part of your day. There is no announcement, only something shared.
s4.daily.family.6: You and {person} arrange a shared space. You leave room for both of your preferences.
s4.daily.family.7: {person} asks what would help with a small task. You answer plainly instead of hoping it will be guessed.
s4.daily.family.8: You and {person} look at something kept from earlier years. You name one moment you both recognize.
s4.daily.family.9: You ask {person} about a routine you had never questioned. The answer gives it a small history.
s4.daily.family.10: You and {person} disagree about a small arrangement. You name the practical problem without deciding the whole relationship by it.
s4.daily.family.11: You say thank you to {person} for something specific. The reason matters more than a perfect sentence.
s4.daily.family.12: {person} mentions a preference you did not know. You keep it in mind for a later conversation.
s4.daily.family.13: You and {person} finish part of an unfinished task. You stop before turning an ordinary day into a deadline.
s4.daily.family.14: You sit nearby while {person} does something familiar. You notice how much of knowing a person happens quietly.
s4.daily.family.15: You and {person} decide what can wait. Leaving one thing undone gives the rest of the day more room.
s4.daily.family.16: {person} asks about an earlier choice of yours. You explain what you knew at the time.
s4.daily.family.17: You and {person} keep a small shared object. You remember what was happening when it first mattered.
s4.daily.family.18: You share a quiet pause with {person}. It does not need to become a lesson or a photograph.
s4.daily.family.19: You tell {person} what you can and cannot arrange this time. A clear answer replaces an uncertain promise.
s4.daily.family.20: You keep a detail from a conversation with {person}. The memory has a person attached to it, not only an age.
s4.daily.work.1: A task is returned with one practical question. You clarify the question before starting the work again.
s4.daily.work.2: You finish a small part of a larger task. You mark what is complete instead of claiming the whole project is done.
s4.daily.work.3: You ask for the information a task needs. The request takes a little courage but prevents more guessing.
s4.daily.work.4: A familiar method stops working well. You test one small change before replacing everything.
s4.daily.work.5: You explain an unfinished piece of work clearly. Naming what remains makes the next step easier to arrange.
s4.daily.work.6: You keep a useful note from a difficult task. It records a method, not a promise that every problem will be easy.
s4.daily.work.7: You notice one repeated inconvenience at work. You write down a possible improvement and its limits.
s4.daily.work.8: You ask which part of a request matters most. A shorter answer changes how you use the remaining time.
s4.daily.work.9: You acknowledge a mistake in a work task. You describe what you can correct without making an unlimited promise.
s4.daily.work.10: You finish the work you agreed to do. You leave a clear handover for the part that belongs to another task.
s4.daily.work.11: You learn a small practical skill during a task. Its value is visible in one thing that now takes less effort.
s4.daily.work.12: You compare the estimate with how long a task actually took. You leave a more honest note for next time.
s4.daily.work.13: You put a boundary around an extra request. Saying what fits makes the help more definite.
s4.daily.work.14: You revisit an early piece of your work. You can recognize both what you learned and what was difficult then.
s4.daily.work.15: You prepare one question before a work conversation. It helps you ask for something more specific than approval.
s4.daily.work.16: You divide a task into smaller parts. One part can begin even though the full plan is not settled.
s4.daily.work.17: You write down who needs which information. An ordinary clarification prevents a needless round of work.
s4.daily.work.18: You complete a repair to a routine process. You keep a note of what changed and what did not.
s4.daily.work.19: You end a work conversation with an agreed next step. It is a commitment of a known size.
s4.daily.work.20: You put away the materials at the end of a task. You allow a finished part to be finished for today.
s4.daily.home.1: You move one everyday object to a better place. The room begins to work a little more easily for you.
s4.daily.home.2: You prepare something simple for yourself. Paying attention to the small process changes how the pause feels.
s4.daily.home.3: You sort a drawer and keep one unexpected object. You can say why it still belongs here.
s4.daily.home.4: You leave one part of the day unplanned. You use it without having to turn it into an achievement.
s4.daily.home.5: You repair a small inconvenience at home. It changes a repeated moment rather than the whole of life.
s4.daily.home.6: You choose a place for something you want to remember. Seeing it becomes a quiet part of the room.
s4.daily.home.7: You try a different route through an ordinary day. You notice one thing the usual routine missed.
s4.daily.home.8: You put an unfinished task where you can return to it. It does not have to occupy the whole room.
s4.daily.home.9: You keep a small ritual that is yours. Today you do it without asking it to solve everything.
s4.daily.home.10: You compare what you use with what you only keep moving around. One small decision makes the space clearer.
s4.daily.home.11: You take time over an ordinary meal. For a while, it is allowed to be the main thing you are doing.
s4.daily.home.12: You open a window or move toward the light. You notice the room before returning to the next task.
s4.daily.home.13: You label a box you had meant to sort. Naming what is inside becomes a manageable beginning.
s4.daily.home.14: You choose which small task can wait. Keeping a limit makes room for the rest of the day.
s4.daily.home.15: You return to an object you once set aside. You decide where it fits in the life you have now.
s4.daily.home.16: You notice a sound that belongs to an ordinary day. Later you want to keep the scene, not only the task.
s4.daily.home.17: You finish one small repair without replacing everything around it. Enough can be a practical decision.
s4.daily.home.18: You make a little space for something you enjoy. It remains a part of the room even when no one sees it.
s4.daily.home.19: You put a useful note somewhere visible. An ordinary reminder makes one return to a task easier.
s4.daily.home.20: You end a quiet part of the day by putting one thing away. The small ending feels complete enough.
s4.daily.wellbeing.1: You notice that you need a pause and take one. You record a rest, not a promise about future health.
s4.daily.wellbeing.2: You leave a small gap between two tasks. The next thing does not have to begin immediately.
s4.daily.wellbeing.3: You choose an easier version of a planned activity. Adjusting it lets you take part at your own pace.
s4.daily.wellbeing.4: You notice where a routine has become uncomfortable. You make one practical adjustment and see how it feels.
s4.daily.wellbeing.5: You put a difficult task down for a while. You leave a note about returning instead of forcing a conclusion.
s4.daily.wellbeing.6: You spend a quiet interval without adding another obligation. The pause does not need to be productive.
s4.daily.wellbeing.7: You pay attention to how an activity feels today. You adjust the plan rather than comparing with another day.
s4.daily.wellbeing.8: You choose one manageable thing from a long list. Completing it does not make the rest disappear, but gives you a place to stop.
s4.daily.wellbeing.9: You take a short walk or move gently within the space available. You notice something beyond the task you were doing.
s4.daily.wellbeing.10: You make a plan smaller after noticing your limits. The revised plan belongs to the day you actually have.
s4.daily.wellbeing.11: You leave an unfinished question unanswered for now. You can keep the question without carrying it through every task.
s4.daily.wellbeing.12: You choose a quieter setting for a little while. You return to the day after giving the pause some room.
s4.daily.wellbeing.13: You notice one source of unnecessary hurry. Removing a small deadline changes the next part of the day.
s4.daily.wellbeing.14: You make it easier to begin a routine task. Moving one object can be more useful than demanding more willpower.
s4.daily.wellbeing.15: You pause before accepting another optional task. You check what you already agreed to do.
s4.daily.wellbeing.16: You take care of a simple need before another task. For today, that order makes sense.
s4.daily.wellbeing.17: You notice the difference between a difficult day and a judgment about your whole life. You record the day as it was.
s4.daily.wellbeing.18: You try an activity in a gentler way. Choosing a limit lets it remain something you can return to.
s4.daily.wellbeing.19: You stop measuring one quiet interval by what you achieved. You keep one detail of what you noticed instead.
s4.daily.wellbeing.20: You choose a stopping point before you are completely worn out. One task remains for another day.
s4.daily.reflection.1: You open an earlier record from this life. Knowing what came later does not erase what you knew then.
s4.daily.reflection.2: You keep an ordinary moment beside a major turning point. Both took real space in the life you lived.
s4.daily.reflection.3: You revisit a choice that did not resolve everything. You can name what it did change.
s4.daily.reflection.4: You find a record of an unfinished plan. You keep the unfinished part instead of inventing a conclusion.
s4.daily.reflection.5: You place an earlier attempt beside a later one. The difference is more specific than success or failure.
s4.daily.reflection.6: You reread a moment you chose to keep. One small detail still tells you why it mattered.
s4.daily.reflection.7: You look at a path you actually followed. You leave the unchosen alternatives open rather than claiming to know their endings.
s4.daily.reflection.8: You keep a note about what was uncertain at the time. It makes an old decision easier to understand.
s4.daily.reflection.9: You find an ordinary object connected with an earlier record. The scene returns before any lesson does.
s4.daily.reflection.10: You put two different feelings about an old chapter into words. They do not have to cancel each other.
s4.daily.reflection.11: You choose not to turn an old memory into advice. It can remain one person's experience.
s4.daily.reflection.12: You read a record of a small beginning. The later result does not make the first step inevitable.
s4.daily.reflection.13: You find a detail that never appeared in a score. You decide it still belongs in the story.
s4.daily.reflection.14: You keep a changed plan beside the original one. Adapting was part of what actually happened.
s4.daily.reflection.15: You notice a gap in the record. You leave it visible instead of filling it with a story you cannot support.
s4.daily.reflection.16: You revisit the reason behind an earlier boundary. The limit made sense in a particular part of life.
s4.daily.reflection.17: You choose a small scene as a first page. You do not ask it to explain every chapter that followed.
s4.daily.reflection.18: You keep an old question alongside a later answer. The distance between them belongs to the story too.
s4.daily.reflection.19: You read an earlier chapter without rushing to rewrite it. Understanding can be different from correcting.
s4.daily.reflection.20: You gather a few recorded moments into one place. What you keep is this particular life, with its open questions.
s4.small-courage.prompt: The pieces are still on the table. Someone nearby can help, but you also want to see what your own hands can do. Where will you begin?
s4.small-courage.preludeTitle: A toy you tried to mend
s4.small-courage.setup: A favorite toy has come apart. You keep its pieces together instead of throwing them away.
s4.small-courage.a.result: You try several arrangements and keep the pieces that fit. The toy is not perfect, but part of the repair is yours.
s4.small-courage.a.follow: When a small task goes wrong later, you remember that trying slowly can be a beginning.
s4.small-courage.b: Ask someone to work beside me
s4.small-courage.b.result: You ask for help and hold a piece while the other person shows you where it goes.
s4.small-courage.b.follow: You keep a memory of being helped without having to hide what you did not know.
s4.small-courage.c: Keep it safely and return another day
s4.small-courage.c.result: You place the pieces in a box. Today you choose another game; the unfinished toy is still yours.
s4.small-courage.c.follow: You find the box again. You can keep an unfinished thing without judging the whole day by it.
s4.school-friend.prompt: {person} is alone during a break. You recognize the person who laughed with you earlier. What would feel possible today?
s4.school-friend.preludeTitle: The person at the next desk
s4.school-friend.setup: You and {person} work on the same classroom task. A shared mistake makes both of you laugh.
s4.school-friend.a.result: You make room in the game and explain the rules. Joining takes a little time, but you start together.
s4.school-friend.a.follow: You and {person} recognize one another more easily now; that first invitation has become a shared memory.
s4.school-friend.b: Sit nearby and start with one question
s4.school-friend.b.result: You sit nearby and ask about the classroom task. A short answer becomes a short conversation.
s4.school-friend.b.follow: You and {person} sometimes begin a conversation with that same ordinary question.
s4.school-friend.c: Offer a greeting and keep some space
s4.school-friend.c.result: You greet {person} and leave the nearby seat free. Today there is no longer conversation.
s4.school-friend.c.follow: You still recognize {person}. A greeting can remain a greeting, without a friendship being owed.
s4.first-interest: Something you want to take seriously
s4.first-interest.prompt: An informal activity gives you a place to share {interest}. Other plans already fill some of your time. How much room do you want to make?
s4.first-interest.preludeTitle: A page that was not homework
s4.first-interest.setup: You begin {interest} in a spare part of the day. There is no grade for it, and you return to it once more.
s4.first-interest.a.result: You reserve a small part of your week for {interest}. Another leisure activity gets less time for now.
s4.first-interest.a.follow: You have a few pieces of practice to look back on. Your interest has a place in the week, even without a prize.
s4.first-interest.b.result: You bring one unfinished attempt to the activity. You listen to a response without promising to make this your whole life.
s4.first-interest.b.follow: You remember being seen while you were still learning. That response stays with your early work.
s4.first-interest.c.result: You keep {interest} in your own notebook and keep the current plans. The activity passes without you.
s4.first-interest.c.follow: You find your early notebook again. Keeping something private was also a choice you made.
s4.words-at-home.prompt: {person} asks how things have been. You remember the conversation you stopped halfway. What would you like to share this time?
s4.words-at-home.setup: While talking with {person}, you stop just before saying what you have been thinking about your next chapter.
s4.words-at-home.a: Say what I hope for, even if it is uncertain
s4.words-at-home.a.result: You tell {person} one hope and one uncertainty. There is no instant agreement, but the words have been heard.
s4.words-at-home.a.follow: A later conversation with {person} has somewhere to begin: you can refer to what you said instead of starting from silence.
s4.words-at-home.b: Ask about them, then share one small thing
s4.words-at-home.b.result: You ask about {person}, then share one small part of your own life. You leave the larger question open.
s4.words-at-home.b.follow: You and {person} have one more ordinary thing to ask about when you next speak.
s4.words-at-home.c.result: You write the rest of the sentence for yourself. It is not sent, and you do not count it as a conversation.
s4.words-at-home.c.follow: The unsent page helps you see what you meant. Whether to share it remains your decision.
s4.old-friend: The message you have not sent
s4.old-friend.prompt: You have a way to contact {person}. You could say hello without knowing whether the old ease will return. What would you like to do?
s4.old-friend.preludeTitle: A familiar name in an old notebook
s4.old-friend.setup: You find a note from the years when you knew {person}. The last contact you recorded was at age {lastAge}.
s4.old-friend.a: Send a personal memory and ask how they are
s4.old-friend.a.result: You send {person} a memory you actually shared. You leave room for a reply rather than asking for the old friendship back at once.
s4.old-friend.a.follow: {person} replies with a detail you had forgotten. Your conversation begins again, with room for how both lives have changed.
s4.old-friend.b.result: You send a short greeting to {person}. It asks for very little and does not pretend the missing years never happened.
s4.old-friend.b.follow: {person} sends a brief reply. You keep a modest connection instead of recreating the whole past.
s4.old-friend.c: Keep the memory without making contact
s4.old-friend.c.result: You close the notebook without sending a message. The old connection is remembered, not renewed.
s4.old-friend.c.follow: You come across the notebook again. It still holds that earlier chapter, without an invented reply.
s4.return-interest: There is still a place to begin
s4.return-interest.prompt: A small local activity welcomes beginners in {interest}. Taking part would use some of the time you now keep free. You do not know how it will go.
s4.return-interest.setup: After starting work, you put your materials for {interest} away and recorded a pause. Now you find them again.
s4.return-interest.a: Join and protect some practice time
s4.return-interest.a.result: You sign up and reserve time to prepare. One free-time plan is postponed; you have made a real place for {interest}.
s4.return-interest.a.follow: You complete a first attempt at the activity. It is uneven, but you now have an experience beyond imagining whether you could begin.
s4.return-interest.b.result: You attend once and watch how others learn. You have not committed to the full activity.
s4.return-interest.b.follow: You bring home one idea to try privately. Learning what the activity was like has become a small step of its own.
s4.return-interest.c: Keep it as a private interest
s4.return-interest.c.result: You keep the original schedule and set the materials somewhere you can reach. You do not enroll.
s4.return-interest.c.follow: On an unhurried day you use those materials privately. This interest does not need an audience to belong to your life.
s4.family-time: Two things you do not want to miss
s4.family-time.prompt: You cannot give the same time to both plans. {person} has invited you; the work request is still open. How will you arrange this?
s4.family-time.setup: {person} suggests sharing an ordinary meal. You also have a work commitment that needs an answer.
s4.family-time.a: Accept the meal and decline the extra request
s4.family-time.a.result: You decline the extra request and share the meal with {person}. The work opportunity is not added to your schedule.
s4.family-time.a.follow: You and {person} later recall a small moment from that meal. The memory is specific because you were both there.
s4.family-time.b: Agree on another time before answering work
s4.family-time.b.result: You tell {person} about the conflict and agree on a different time. You record a plan, not a visit that has already happened.
s4.family-time.b.follow: You keep the rearranged meeting with {person}. Asking clearly made the change possible; the first plan was still missed.
s4.family-time.c: Take the work request and explain honestly
s4.family-time.c.result: You accept the work request and tell {person} that you will miss the meal. You do not promise another date you have not arranged.
s4.family-time.c.follow: You remember how you handled two competing commitments. Missing this meal does not decide the worth of the whole relationship.
s4.work-boundary: What can you promise this time
s4.work-boundary.prompt: Helping is possible, but the extra time would come from your own plans. How much can you honestly offer?
s4.work-boundary.preludeTitle: Another request at the end of the day
s4.work-boundary.setup: At work, you receive a request to help beyond the task you had agreed to finish. You have already completed your planned work.
s4.work-boundary.a: Help this time, with a clear stopping point
s4.work-boundary.a.result: You offer a limited amount of help and name the stopping point. A personal plan is shortened.
s4.work-boundary.a.follow: You complete the agreed part of the help. Naming its limit keeps this one request from becoming an unlimited promise.
s4.work-boundary.b: Discuss what can wait until another day
s4.work-boundary.b.result: You explain your availability and help separate the urgent part from what can wait.
s4.work-boundary.b.follow: The work is divided into smaller commitments. Negotiating the request becomes part of doing the work well.
s4.work-boundary.c: Decline and keep the original plans
s4.work-boundary.c.result: You decline the extra request politely. Someone else will need to arrange that work; your personal time remains yours.
s4.work-boundary.c.follow: You remember one occasion when you kept a boundary without needing to turn the other person into a villain.
s4.shared-time: Make room for the two of you
s4.shared-time.prompt: You can name a small thing to do together, rather than waiting for a perfect free week. What would you like to propose?
s4.shared-time.preludeTitle: A plan you wrote down together
s4.shared-time.setup: You and {person} write down one small thing you would like to do together. It is a plan, not yet a shared outing.
s4.shared-time.a: Set aside time for the original plan
s4.shared-time.a.result: You and {person} set aside time and complete the small plan. Another optional activity is left for later.
s4.shared-time.a.follow: You now share a memory of doing the thing, instead of only talking about doing it someday.
s4.shared-time.b: Suggest a simpler version for today
s4.shared-time.b.result: You and {person} choose a simpler version and do it together. The larger plan is still open.
s4.shared-time.b.follow: You remember that an ordinary shared hour could count without being a perfect occasion.
s4.shared-time.c: Talk about why the plan keeps slipping
s4.shared-time.c.result: You and {person} talk about what has been taking your attention. You do not record an outing that has not happened.
s4.shared-time.c.follow: You have a clearer conversation to refer to when deciding what to arrange next.
s4.friend-repair: Leave it there, or try another sentence
s4.friend-repair.prompt: You remember both the awkward exchange and the earlier years you shared with {person}. What would be honest to do next?
s4.friend-repair.preludeTitle: A message that felt harder to answer
s4.friend-repair.setup: In a conversation you renewed with {person}, one short exchange ends awkwardly. You leave it unanswered for now.
s4.friend-repair.a: Explain what I meant and leave space for a reply
s4.friend-repair.a.result: You explain one thing you meant without deciding what {person} must have intended.
s4.friend-repair.a.follow: A later reply clears up part of the misunderstanding. Not every difference disappears, but one sentence becomes easier to understand.
s4.friend-repair.b: Ask how the exchange felt to them
s4.friend-repair.b.result: You ask {person} about the exchange and listen before writing another explanation.
s4.friend-repair.b.follow: You learn a detail about how the conversation landed. Listening changes what you choose to say next.
s4.friend-repair.c.result: You choose not to send another message now. The disagreement is not recorded as resolved.
s4.friend-repair.c.follow: You remember choosing space. The record keeps the unanswered part rather than inventing a reconciliation.
s4.later-letter: What would you keep from this chapter
s4.later-letter.prompt: You can write about a choice you made, something you learned, or an ordinary moment worth keeping. Where would you begin?
s4.later-letter.preludeTitle: A page for someone still learning
s4.later-letter.setup: You set aside a page to write about an experience you actually lived through, without turning it into advice for everyone.
s4.later-letter.a: Write honestly about a difficult choice
s4.later-letter.a.result: You write about an earlier recorded choice, including what you could not know at the time.
s4.later-letter.a.follow: The page gives your earlier self some context instead of judging the choice only by what came afterward.
s4.later-letter.b: Keep an ordinary moment in detail
s4.later-letter.b.result: You describe one earlier recorded moment, keeping the small details rather than claiming a grand lesson.
s4.later-letter.b.follow: You can return to a particular scene from this life, not only a list of achievements.
s4.later-letter.c: Leave a page open and keep the record
s4.later-letter.c.result: You leave the page open and keep the earlier record. Today you do not need to finish interpreting your life.
s4.later-letter.c.follow: The open page remains part of the collection. You can keep a life without reducing it to one lesson.
s4.memory-box: Choose a first page for the collection
s4.memory-box.prompt: There is no need to know how the rest of life will unfold. Looking at what has already happened, how would you begin telling this story?
s4.memory-box.setup: You gather a few records from this life: things you chose and moments you decided to keep.
s4.memory-box.a.result: You place an earlier choice at the beginning of the collection, keeping its actual outcome beside it.
s4.memory-box.a.follow: The collection now begins with a decision in context. It does not claim that one choice explains your whole life.
s4.memory-box.b: Begin with an ordinary moment I kept
s4.memory-box.b.result: You place a recorded moment at the beginning. The smaller scene is allowed to matter.
s4.memory-box.b.follow: Your collection leaves room for what was lived, alongside what could be measured.
s4.memory-box.c: Keep the chapters in the order they happened
s4.memory-box.c.result: You keep the recorded order instead of choosing one event to stand for everything.
s4.memory-box.c.follow: The collection remains a sequence of chapters, with room for mixed feelings and unfinished questions.
